---
title: "02 · Simple regression"
subtitle: "Week 1"
---

::: {.guiding-q}
How does one variable predict another?
:::

## In this session

- Least squares: fitting a line with `lm()`
- Interpreting intercept, slope and residual standard deviation
- Inference: standard errors, confidence intervals, *t*- and *p*-values
- Assumptions and diagnostics: residual plots, influential cases
- Reporting a regression result

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Intercept](../../glossary.qmd#intercept), [Residuals](../../glossary.qmd#residuals), [Standard error](../../glossary.qmd#standard-error), [Confidence interval](../../glossary.qmd#confidence-interval), [*p*-value](../../glossary.qmd#p-value), [Assumptions (of the linear model)](../../glossary.qmd#assumptions), [Heteroscedasticity](../../glossary.qmd#heteroscedasticity), [Influential cases](../../glossary.qmd#influential-cases), [Cook's distance](../../glossary.qmd#cooks-distance)
:::

## Learning goals

After this session you can

- fit a simple regression in R and interpret its coefficients,
- explain what a standard error and a confidence interval mean,
- check model assumptions with diagnostic plots.

## Simulate first

If we simulate data from a known model again and again, the estimated slopes scatter around the true value. Their spread *is* the standard error.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
set.seed(2)
true_b1 <- 0.8
slopes <- replicate(2000, {
  age  <- runif(30, 1, 10)
  mass <- 3 + true_b1 * age + rnorm(30, 0, 1.5)
  coef(lm(mass ~ age))[2]
})

hist(slopes, breaks = 40, col = "#1b6f8a", border = "white",
     main = "Sampling distribution of the slope", xlab = "Estimated slope")
abline(v = true_b1, col = "#c0392b", lwd = 2)
sd(slopes)   # compare with the SE that summary(lm(...)) reports for one sample
```
